CHIEF COMPLAINT
Asthma exacerbations with sports and mood concerns.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a student who reports a longstanding history of asthma that has been limiting his ability to participate in water polo. He experiences symptoms primarily with aerobic activity and sports, occurring nearly every time he engages in such exercise. He describes chest tightness, wheezing, phlegm buildup in throat, coughing, and lightheadedness. He uses a two-puff albuterol inhaler when symptomatic, which provides some relief of the phlegm sensation but still requires him to sit down and rest for approximately 15 minutes to fully recover. He experiences tremor/shakiness with the inhaler, which was discussed as a normal side effect. He denies nocturnal awakening from asthma symptoms. He is also triggered by cigarette smoke exposure. He is not currently on any daily asthma medications. Additionally, patient reports mood symptoms that began at the start of the current school year. He describes feeling stressed about SAT preparation and AP classes. He reports significant sadness, lack of motivation, fatigue, and social withdrawal—friends invite him out but he prefers to stay home. He initially tried to join sports hoping to feel more energized and happy but these symptoms have persisted.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for exercise-induced cough and wheezing, smoke-triggered cough, fatigue, and mood changes. Patient reports seasonal allergies. Denies nocturnal cough or sleep disruption from asthma.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Asthma
Seasonal allergies

MEDICATIONS
Albuterol inhaler 2 puffs as needed

Not documented

Vital signs: Not documented

RESULTS
Physical examination findings as documented above. Mild serous otitis noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Asthma, exercise-induced with possible allergic component: Will start daily montelukast (Singulair) to provide baseline control. Patient to continue using albuterol inhaler as needed for acute symptoms. Discussed that tremor is an expected side effect of albuterol; recommend continuing to sit down for recovery after use. Follow-up appointment in 6 weeks to assess response to Singulair.

2. Mood disorder/depression, likely stress-related: New onset at beginning of school year, appearing related to academic pressures. Recommend starting therapy with a mental health professional. Will complete screening questionnaires. Follow-up in 2 weeks.
